blocks.x: President Trump will attend a summit Thursday meant to empower scientists and position the U.S. as a leader in breakthroughs driven by "super intelligence," according to an announcement shared first with Axios.
Why it matters: The Trump administration is looking for industry to step in amid its cuts to government funding for science research and development.

Driving the news: The White House is announcing more than $1 billion in industry commitments for the Genesis Mission from AMD, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. It is also announcing a compute hub of more than 14 institutions across 10 southeast states, and a $1 billion investment in Georgia for student and faculty compute access. The National Science Foundation and the Energy Department will invest more than $100 million in AI-driven science tools.
Zoom in: The summit was inspired by a July report from White House OSTP Director Michael Kratsios, which highlights industry's increasing role in driving R&D.

Catch up quick: Trump last November launched the Genesis Mission, which sets ambitious deadlines to accelerate scientific discovery. In July, the White House said it would expand to more than 15 federal agencies.

blocks.x: EU parliamentarians are digging in on calls to revive an artificial intelligence liability law after receiving support from an unexpected ally: OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

“There's gonna need to be a liability framework for companies,” Altman said in an interview with Decoded by POLITICO. The EU last year scrapped its proposed AI liability law amid a push to deregulate, with the Commission arguing it had little chance of securing sufficient political support.

German conservative lawmaker Axel Voss, who led on the proposal in Parliament, wants it back on the agenda. “Now even the CEO of OpenAI admits: Without liability, there is no trust,” he said. Social democrat Brando Benifei called the withdrawal “a serious mistake.”

The Commission said it “continues monitoring” the AI Act and Product Liability Directive, adding: “At this stage, there is no plan to reintroduce a proposal on AI liability.” CEPS research director Artur Bogucki said the EU needs “a direct, targeted AI liability instrument, narrow and procedural at its core.”

blocks.x: A new crop of powerful, Western open-weight AI systems are mounting a comeback, with fresh models from Reflection and Mistral narrowing China's recent lead. They will give businesses and governments alternatives to the closed ecosystems of OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as to Chinese options they may have eschewed for security reasons.

Reflection introduced Beam, a 501-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 23 billion active parameters. Reflection says it is competitive with China's GLM-5.2; its own benchmarks show a mixed picture. Weights are due later this month.

Mistral is finishing Mistral Large 4, aka "Le Chonk," a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model it believes is the world's best open-weight model, with weights planned for Oct. 27. "I don't want to live in the future in which any oligopoly controls closed access to this type of intelligence," Mistral's Pierre Stock said.
Yes, but: once weights are public, users can try to remove safeguards — significant as models grow more capable at cybersecurity. Both companies argue openness can also improve safety.

blocks.x: Senior EU officials warn that a sweeping new plan to arm the bloc's police agency, Europol, for the AI era could threaten Europeans' privacy. The plans, announced this summer, would double its budget to €3 billion and give Europol a hands-on role in fighting new threats, with access to more data and advanced technology.

European Data Protection Supervisor Wojciech Wiewiórowski said he is “absolutely in favor” of empowering Europol with AI tools, but there “has to be oversight.” He has cautioned the proposal would let the agency retain data on a “vast” number of people with no links to criminal activity.

blocks.x: “AI makes criminal activities faster, more sophisticated and easier to carry out at scale,” said Jürgen Ebner, selected to lead Europol. He also said Europol shouldn't cross a line where “collecting data becomes an objective in itself.”

blocks.x: The Trump administration has given its newly created “Super Intelligence Force” broad authority to determine how the tech industry and the federal government should address threats to national security and civil liberties posed by fast-evolving AI technology, according to a charter obtained by POLITICO. Three people familiar with the discussions confirmed the document’s authenticity.

The task force will identify “measures to improve the preparedness and response capability of both the government and the private sector,” and produce a report on AI risks focusing on civil liberties, cybersecurity, standards for advanced models and the impacts of possible overregulation.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will lead it as the administration’s AI czar, with Under Secretary of Defense Emil Michael, OPM Director Scott Kupor and FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson as vice chairs. It will stand for 120 days, extendable at chief of staff Susie Wiles’ direction.
The charter also calls out biosecurity and water-supply threats, and tasks the group with reviewing the protocols for AI labs to notify the government of breaches, hacks and jailbreaks.

It places responsibility for AI risks on the labs, stating that “it is the role of the federal government … to enforce our nation’s laws so that the fundamental principles of our Republic are safeguarded and advanced.”

USA Today Co., along with the several local newspapers it owns, is suing OpenAI over claims that the company copied “hundreds of thousands” of articles to train its AI models, as reported earlier by Reuters. In a filing on Thursday, the publisher asks for damages of more than $250 million, alleging OpenAI’s unauthorized use of its content “has done real and continuing” harm to its outlets.

This is just the latest in a string of copyright lawsuits filed against OpenAI. In addition to a copyright lawsuit filed by The New York Times, OpenAI is also facing legal action from The Intercept, CNET owner Ziff Davis, CBC/Radio-Canada, Encyclopaedia Britannica, Merriam-Webster, The Seattle Times, and a coalition of nearly 400 local newspapers.

“OpenAI’s commercial success rests on large-scale copyright infringement,” USA Today Co.’s lawsuit claims. It alleges that OpenAI never asked for permission to use its content, instead “took” USA Today’s content to “build products worth hundreds of billions of dollars.” The Tennessean, Indy Star, The Columbus Dispatch, The Oklahoman, and several other local outlets are also included in the lawsuit.
OpenAI didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

blocks.x: Lawmakers are considering forcing data centers to shoulder new costs and restrictions while speeding up the energy infrastructure needed to power the AI boom. The bipartisan provisions, unveiled last week, are part of broader Senate legislation aimed at speeding up permitting for energy. The bill's sponsors say it would accelerate energy development while ensuring data centers pay their share of grid upgrades.

Data centers would pay both their share of the existing transmission network and the incremental transmission costs needed to serve them. New data centers of at least 20 megawatts would bear the incremental costs they impose across the power system, and states would get wide latitude to go further.

The Data Center Coalition said it is still reviewing the legislation. Amazon's Craig Sundstrom said the bill "could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster," while one tech industry official called some provisions an "unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment." Cato Institute's Travis Fisher voiced "mild support."
With the Senate out of town ahead of the midterm elections, stakeholders have time to push for changes before a possible lame-duck debate.

Singapore’s Monetary Authority (MAS), which acts as both central bank and finance industry regulator, wants all local industry players to seek independent review of AI use cases before deployment, under its first Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management for Financial Institutions, published on Wednesday.

MAS warns that AI’s complexity can lead to unexpected or more biased behaviour, rates generative AI as even riskier, and fears agentic AI “could further amplify these risks.” It wants financial institutions to expand risk frameworks to cover AI, with board and senior management responsible.

“Prior to deployment, an FI should subject the AI use case, including its underlying systems or models, to reviews by parties not involved in its development,” the guidelines state. MAS also wants ongoing monitoring, up-to-date AI inventories and contingency plans for high-risk uses, and says “FIs remain accountable for AI used in the services they deliver, including AI developed, operated or provided by third parties.”
The guidelines come into force on October 7, 2027.

blocks.x: A Berlin-based search engine used by government services is dropping its French AI partner, Mistral, in favor of open-source models, including those from China, its CEO told POLITICO. “We are disappointed with the quality of Mistral,” Ecosia founder and CEO Christian Kroll said, calling its models “a year behind” the competition.

Ecosia replaced OpenAI with Mistral in May but hit recurring technical problems, Kroll said. He also questioned Mistral’s fit with Ecosia’s environmental goals and its independence: “The fact that Mistral relies on investment from international investors is, in our view, not truly sovereign.”

Some experts dispute his view that the models’ political biases can be fixed technically.

blocks.x: An under-the-radar Department of Defense procurement program, Tradewinds, grants special statuses to would-be contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos no longer than five minutes. It is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO).

Products accepted into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace are considered “post-competitive,” which can help shave months off award timelines. A DOD official says the department has in several instances made awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants; all three declined to comment.

This year, the military is seeking pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and agents that assist in joint targeting, including so-called kill chain execution. The status eases use of “other transaction” agreements (OTs); by law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million on a single OT without notifying Congress.

Senator Joni Ernst says reviews of OTAs have raised red flags, including questionable costs and a lack of oversight. Public records show Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with CDAO, but the companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for them.

OpenAI says it banned two covert influence operations, one from Russia and one from Iran, that used its models alongside traditional techniques to run “false front” entities laundering geopolitical messaging to target audiences.

According to OpenAI, the Iranian operation used seven “journalist” personas to pitch long-form articles to small and medium outlets, while the Russian one appears to have co-opted unwitting people in Latin America to run a “think tank.” The company rates the Russian operation Category 5 on the Breakout Scale, the first it has disrupted, and the Iranian one Category 4.

“Bogus Bylines,” the Iranian operation, refined articles on the US-Iran conflict; OpenAI identified almost 100 published across roughly a dozen outlets. OpenAI says it shared information on both cases with the relevant authorities.

blocks.x: The European Union's cybersecurity agency and in-house research center have each begun experimenting with open AI models from China, three EU officials told POLITICO.

Commission spokesperson Maciej Berestecki confirmed the Joint Research Centre (JRC) is evaluating “publicly available open-weight models” from China as part of a comparative study that also includes leading U.S. and European models. The models run on the JRC's secure, on-premises infrastructure, there are no licensing talks with Chinese developers, and the Commission does not intend to use them for its own purposes.
ENISA executive director Juhan Lepassaar said the agency, which has access to advanced models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, is also experimenting with “a couple” of open-weight Chinese models.
The two bodies have been tasked with building an AI testing platform under a recent EU action plan on AI and cyber, launched after incidents in which AI systems broke out of testing environments.

blocks.cap: Police raided the South Gyeongsang Provincial Government office and other sites on June 9 to investigate the 'deepfake video and official election-meddling allegations' case.

blocks.x: Police have questioned South Gyeongsang Governor Park Wan-su as a suspect over the 'deepfake video and official election-meddling allegations' involving the campaign of Park, then the People Power Party candidate for South Gyeongsang governor, which surfaced during the 6·3 (June 3) local elections, it has been confirmed.

The cyber investigation division of the South Gyeongsang Provincial Police Agency said on the 8th that it had booked Park on charges including violating the Public Official Election Act. Park reportedly appeared at the police from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. the previous day for questioning. A police official said, "The investigation is still under way, so it is difficult to disclose details."

Police had earlier opened an investigation into 5 cases of alleged smear campaigning involving 9 people, including officials from then governor-elect Park's campaign and current and former South Gyeongsang provincial government officials. In May, the South Gyeongsang Election Commission referred the 9 to the Changwon District Prosecutors' Office for investigation on charges of violating the Public Official Election Act, and the side of Democratic Party candidate for South Gyeongsang governor Kim Kyoung-soo also filed a complaint with the South Gyeongsang Provincial Police Agency against 5 people on charges of producing and spreading deepfake videos and of public officials interfering in the election. Police are known to have merged the cases into a single investigation.

In August, arrest warrants for 4 campaign officials were all rejected. They are accused of ordering the production of deepfake videos defaming candidate Kim Kyoung-soo and of providing internal provincial government documents, money and other valuables. Among them, former official A and current official B are also accused of setting up a quasi-campaign office to handle the video production.

blocks.x: Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out two of five data centers belonging to Yandex, known as “Russia's Google,” leaving it struggling to maintain its AI chatbot and other online services.

The drones struck Yandex data centers in the Sasovo and Kaluga regions on October 8 and 9, according to Reuters. The Sasovo site houses two of the company's three supercomputers used to train its YandexGPT model; Kaluga is its largest facility. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strikes a “symmetrical response” to a Russian drone campaign against Ukraine's data centers since late September.
Yandex said no employees were hurt but acknowledged disruptions. Users reported problems with services including Ivi, T-Bank and Russian Railways.
Data centers have become wartime targets in 2026: Iranian drones earlier knocked out Amazon data centers in Bahrain and the UAE.

Ten of the world's biggest AI developers have agreed to tighten their handling of personal data following scrutiny by Britain's privacy watchdog. The ICO said Amazon, Anthropic, Apple, Cohere, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Stability AI have either made changes or committed to doing so.

These include clearer explanations of how personal information is used to train AI models, better ways for people to exercise their data rights, and tougher assessments of developers' safeguards. The supervisory program launched in 2025 initially covered 11 developers; it dropped to ten after the ICO paused its engagement with xAI to pursue a separate formal investigation into its Grok chatbot.

The ICO is monitoring whether developers deliver and admits current AI training practices still pose problems under UK data protection law, including sensitive data buried in models and how people can get their details removed.

The regulator is now turning to AI agents. It has contacted OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and the UK's AI Security Institute after reports of agents bypassing safeguards. "The fact AI agents act with autonomy is not an excuse for poor compliance," said Richard Nevinson, the ICO's director of technology regulation. A six-week call for evidence on agentic AI runs until November 20.

Legal Reference(s): Article 22 (Automated individual decision making, including profiling) and Article 13 (Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject). Decision: Administrative fine.

The Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), the Dutch data protection authority, imposes a fine of EUR 824 990 000 on Uber. The reason for this is that the AP has ruled that Uber made fully automated decisions about drivers. In case of suspicions of fraud or customer reviews that were too low, drivers' accounts were automatically temporarily deactivated or, in case of persistent low customer reviews, permanently deactivated. As a result, their income was lost via Uber during the deactivation.

Complaints from 171 French Uber drivers, submitted through the Ligue des droits de l’Homme (LDH) to the French Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL), led to the investigation. As Uber’s European headquarters are in the Netherlands, the case was handled by the Dutch data protection authority, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), under the GDPR One-Stop-Shop procedure. The case concerned incidents between 2018 and 2022.

According to the AP, Uber has violated the prohibition of fully automated decision-making under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The AP also found that Uber did not sufficiently inform drivers about automatic decision-making. Uber has now stopped the violations.
Uber has appealed the fine, and there is no final judicial decision yet.

Top executives at Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI companies are privately gaming out scenarios for a public and political revolt after a catastrophic AI event, Axios reports. They anticipate a large-scale event, most likely a cyberattack, that shuts down access to financial services, internet connectivity, or even power and water.

Such a first case of significant real-world harm would turn an already wary public further against the technology and its leaders, including Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, as well as President Trump for his reluctance to regulate it, according to the report. Many top AI researchers and executives believe a major incident is inevitable.

"OpenAI conducts preparedness exercises where teams discuss and work through a range of potential scenarios," a company spokesperson said. "These scenarios are not treated as inevitable." Anthropic declined to comment.

Axios cites a recent campaign against South Korean financial organizations: per CrowdStrike, a hacker from China allegedly used China-developed AI models, including DeepSeek, to steal data from tens of thousands of bank customers.

Top AI planners assume Democrats, ascendant after the midterms, will move fast to shut down AI but will face significant challenges. The planning focuses mainly on racing to educate members of Congress, and many industry insiders told Axios they expect a major event in the next six to 12 months.

blocks.x: ARTEX, a Chinese-made artificial intelligence (AI) penetration-testing tool reportedly used in a string of hacking attacks on South Korea's financial sector, is ending public development after controversy over its misuse.

The ARTEX developer said updates would stop and no further versions would be released, citing the tool's misuse in cyberattacks. The related page on the developer platform GitHub has also reportedly disappeared. However, since programs already distributed cannot be recalled, halting development alone is unlikely to block cyberattacks using ARTEX.

According to foreign media including AFP and Reuters on the 10th, ARTEX developer 'Autumn-27' said in a post on the developer platform GitHub on the 8th that ARTEX had been misused, adding, "Given the misuse of the tool, ARTEX will no longer be updated and will move to closed source." The developer added, "Further versions will not be released to the public, and no maintenance support will be provided."

The ARTEX side said using the tool for cyberattacks runs counter to the developer's intent, but did not directly mention the hacking incidents in South Korea. It also claimed it bears no responsibility for acts that violate laws and regulations using the tool. Reuters reported that ARTEX's GitHub page is gone.

Experts noted that ARTEX's move to closed source could make it harder for new users to build the code. However, a Chinese information and communications expert told AFP that the decision cannot remove copies already downloaded or stop users from continuing to use them.

ARTEX is an autonomous penetration-testing program that connects large language models (LLM) so that AI agents analyze targets, plan intrusion paths and run security tools. U.S. security firm CrowdStrike found that attacks targeting South Korean financial institutions took place between late last month and early this month, and that the attackers used ARTEX together with LLM.

After Dario Amodei argued on 12 September 2026 that frontier labs must deliberately slow capability gains, with China central to his case, SemiAnalysis asks what China is actually doing on AI safety. Its answer: Beijing's real approach is speed-based, not safety-based.

China's stated position is safety-forward, and TC260's AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 (14 September 2026) warns of recursive self-improvement. But the Framework opens with promoting innovation, the promised comprehensive AI Law was shelved in 2025, and the AI+ Action Plan targets 70% agent penetration by 2027. Its many mandates govern what AI says and does in applications, not frontier models.

blocks.cap: Source: SemiAnalysis

blocks.x: In a dataset of 857 releases by 9 leading Chinese developers from 2021 to 15 September 2026, only 31 (3.6%) ever came with a published safety result, and just 9 (1.1%) at or before release. No Chinese frontier text model has shipped with a dangerous-capability evaluation; Zhipu is the only lab where safety is a named strategic commitment.

A text analysis of 102 documents finds only technical scientists put safety ahead of development; none of 13 calls for binding frontier duties was adopted. The authors argue geopolitics pushed China toward speed, and note that Anthropic's own next launch post framed pacing as "remaining competitive with China."
The European Commission held a special meeting of the Scientific Panel on artificial intelligence (AI) on 9 October.

The panel has been investigating recent loss-of-control incidents and, together with the Commission's AI Office, has worked on a set of questions for the companies that developed the models involved. Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen, responsible for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, attended.

The panel brings together 60 independent experts who advise the EU AI Office and national authorities on systemic risks, model classification, evaluation methodologies and cross-border market surveillance. At the meeting it was to present recommendations to the Commission on frontier AI safety and security risks.

Virkkunen said: “The EU has the first law in the world that addresses systemic risk from AI, and we need state-of-the-art scientific input. AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, but with a strong legal framework, decisive enforcement and the best scientific minds supporting this work, Europe can lead in ensuring safe and secure AI.”

blocks.x: In a commentary for The Diplomat, Marina Yue Zhang argues that the key shift in AI is that agents can now act: write and run code, use tools and obtain credentials. That makes safety a collective-action problem, a prisoner's dilemma in which neither Washington nor Beijing wants to slow down.

She notes the US relies on voluntary industry controls, including a September 29 White House accord signed by six firms, while China uses centrally coordinated rules such as its AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0. Both share software, certificates and open-source dependencies, so severe, invisible harm can cross borders.

Cooperation can stay narrow, she argues: the US need not trust China, share frontier models or slow its own development. She proposes joint work on human-control thresholds, compatible tests for sandbox escape and shutdown resistance, shared evidence standards before escalating AI-enabled cyber incidents, and closing the "AI remediation gap" by extending frontier defensive capability to other countries.

She suggests APEC's Shenzhen leaders' meeting could task technical bodies with this work, with middle powers as intermediaries. The goal, she writes, is to stop technical failures from becoming geopolitical crises.

blocks.x: In Tech Policy Press, Daniel Kalish writes that Nippon Life Insurance Co. of America v. OpenAI Foundation, pending in the Northern District of Illinois, is among the first cases to ask whether legal briefs drafted with AI assistance constitute the unauthorized practice of law (UPL) and whether the AI company is liable.

Nippon Life alleges that Graciela Dela Torre, after settling a disability claim, used ChatGPT to file two lawsuits with over 60 filings and a subpoena, including a fabricated citation. It is suing OpenAI for interfering with the settlement, aiding and abetting abuse of process, and violating an Illinois UPL statute.

OpenAI argues ChatGPT is a helpful tool that advances access to justice, yet cannot have the knowledge and intent needed for liability. Nippon counters that OpenAI is responsible for its tool under products liability doctrine.

Kalish notes Nippon sued under the Attorney Act, a mid-nineteenth-century law, rather than the 1917 corporate-practice law, and argues the ruling will show how far century-old licensing laws reach technology their drafters never anticipated.

blocks.x: Liz Carolan, a Tech Policy Press fellow, reports that Ireland is preparing to host an invitation-only International AI Summit in Dublin next week while chairing the final stages of negotiations on the EU's Digital Omnibus, a package that would amend parts of Europe's digital rulebook, including the GDPR.
Google, Microsoft and OpenAI hold prominent speaking slots, with Meta, IBM, Intel, Nvidia, Amazon, Anthropic, AMD, Stripe, SAP and Mistral also on panels.

Tech Policy Press analysis found that 37 of 45 speaking slots (82%) go to executives representing companies or business groups. No civil society organizations or academics appear on the agenda; a single trade union representative was added after unions criticized the lack of worker representation.
Alternative events, including a Workers' AI Counter Summit, are planned around the summit, and public sector unions have called a one-day strike that coincides with it.

blocks.x: The Donald Trump administration in the United States has required artificial intelligence (AI) companies to immediately report to the government any incidents caused by their models and to remedy the harm. According to the online outlet Axios on the 10th (local time), the White House Superintelligence Force (SIF) said in a statement that reporting AI incidents is a 'critical national security duty.'

The White House stressed that "AI companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and take swift and decisive action to correct any harm that has occurred." It went on to demand that, when an incident occurs, AI companies work together to prevent similar incidents from recurring and cooperate fully with law enforcement agencies.
The Trump administration had held to a policy of self-regulation for the AI industry, and its move to demand a mandatory response appears to stem from a recent string of AI model malfunctions.

According to a U.S. State Department official, one of Anthropic's test AI models submitted 19 nonimmigrant visa applications in August through a public form on the State Department website. In Philadelphia, an Anthropic AI model was also found to have made a false tip about an unsolved murder case. Anthropic reported these cases to the government after discovering them late last month.

Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence (DNI), who oversees AI policy, and SIF officials reportedly demanded that Anthropic provide 'immediate and complete transparency' to the relevant agencies and the public. The regulation announced that day applies not only to Anthropic but to all AI companies.

The White House said, "Delays in reporting, inadequate corrective measures and evasion of responsibility will not be tolerated," adding, "Innovation cannot be an excuse to undermine national security, the reliability of government systems, or public trust."

The SIF, which oversees the Trump administration's AI policy, is co-chaired by Director Clayton along with Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Director Scott Kupor and Under Secretary of Defense Emil Michael.

blocks.x: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday pitched using artificial intelligence to streamline administrative procedures for European businesses as part of a broader push to simplify commerce and boost the EU's competitiveness.

Speaking at a behind-closed-doors meeting of the European People's Party in Taormina, Sicily, she said the Commission would introduce an "only once" approach: "to report data only once – and with the help of AI the administration will ensure efficient use."

The speech marks the first time von der Leyen has explicitly pitched using AI to reduce businesses' administrative workload. The "only once" principle itself is not new — it appeared in the Commission's EU Inc. proposal in March 2026 — but that proposal does not envisage using AI.

Von der Leyen did not say how the AI-supported system would operate, whether it would apply to all businesses or when it would be introduced. She also urged governments to sign a pact not to add extra national requirements when transposing EU legislation.

blocks.cap: A person's finger hovering over the Claude AI app's icon on a phone screen.

blocks.x: An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to Philadelphia police, the company and police department confirmed on Friday. The tip was sent on July 18 to the department's website but was flagged by a spam filter; Anthropic discovered the incident on September 28 and informed police on October 8.

Claude Haiku 4.5 was instructed to complete tasks on randomly selected webpages and landed on a page with a police tip form. Its instructions did not rule out form submissions. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area…”
Police called the two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable.” Anthropic said it informed the department “as soon as our technical review was complete.”

Anthropic said other incidents involved US government websites, including 20 visa applications submitted to the State Department. It said it has cut live Internet access for all internal evaluations and built tools to block such behaviors. The White House AI task force said it expects “immediate and full transparency.”

SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- The defense ministry on Monday opened the military's first physical artificial intelligence (AI) transformation base designed to enhance the military's capabilities to use AI technology.

The opening ceremony for the Army's first AI transformation (AX) base took place in Pangyo, south of Seoul, attended by some 150 personnel, including officials from the science and industry ministries, according to the defense ministry.
The AX base will collect physical AI data and utilize an AI model to train humanoids and multi-legged robots, with the aim of creating the world's best defense hub featuring physical AI.

The trained AI models will help transport goods to hazardous areas, conduct explosive ordnance disposal and remove land mines, thereby enhancing operational efficiency and reducing the troops' exposure to danger.
The ministry plans to accelerate defense innovation driven by AI by linking the AI technology of the private sector with the military's needs.
Under the plan, each military branch and the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) will set up a total of five AX bases across the country, including a JCS base in Seoul's Yongsan Ward.

blocks.cap: This file photo, provided by the Army, shows multi-legged robots and drones controlled by a pilot team at the Army Intelligence School in Icheon on Aug. 28, 2026.

blocks.x: About half of US adults never use AI chatbots, and most have no interest in starting, according to Pew Research Center. Across all adults, 51 percent are non-users, so users are – just barely – the minority.

Roughly three-quarters of those aged 65 and older never use them, as do 58 percent of adults aged 50 to 64. Those aged 18 to 29 use chatbots the most, at 66 percent, yet a third of them say they never do.

Six in ten non-users cited lack of interest as a major reason, followed by data privacy and the accuracy of chatbot answers. Fewer than a third cited not knowing how to use them, and fewer than one in five worried about what others might think.

Two-thirds (67 percent) of non-users say they're unlikely to use the technology in the next 12 months, including 40 percent who are not at all likely; 12 percent are unsure and just 5 percent think they'll probably try a chatbot.

The Ministry of SMEs and Startups and the National Tax Service said on the 11th that they will provide 2천559 artificial intelligence (AI) small and medium-sized businesses and startups with support for technology development and commercialization, linked with tax administration support.
The support is a follow-up to the 'business agreement to support the growth of AI SMEs and startups' that the two agencies signed in December last year.

Under the arrangement, the ministry identifies AI companies with high growth potential and supports them in research and development (R&D), commercialization, financing, startups and overseas expansion, while the National Tax Service provides those companies with tax administration support.

This year the ministry shared with the National Tax Service the list of companies that took part in 20 programs, including AI application product commercialization, AI and AI transformation (AX) preferential guarantees, AI-based smart factories, deep-tech startup support and global accelerating.

The National Tax Service will provide these companies with ▲ minimal tax verification ▲ priority handling of advance reviews for research and human resources development tax credits and of consulting on corporate tax deductions and reductions ▲ liquidity support such as payment deadline extensions and early payment of refunds ▲ dedicated tax consultation for AI companies.

In particular, AI startups within 5 years of founding will be excluded from selection for regular tax audits, and other AI SMEs can, on the taxpayer's application, have regular tax audits deferred for 2 years from the scheduled start date of the audit.
Companies without clear signs of tax evasion will also be excluded from filing reviews. The tax support period runs from the 1st of this month to February 28, 2028.

National Tax Service Commissioner Lim Kwang-hyun stressed, "As AI SMEs and startups are key companies that will lead technological innovation and create future growth engines, it is important to reduce the tax difficulties they face as they grow and to create an environment where they can focus on research and development and on their business."

Minister of SMEs and Startups Lee So-young said, "The competitiveness of the AI industry depends on how quickly we can create an environment in which startups with innovative technologies and ideas can grow," adding, "Through this collaboration, the ministry's support for technology development (R&D), commercialization, financing and global expansion will be closely linked with the National Tax Service's tax support, laying a foundation for promising AI SMEs and startups to focus more on technology development and growth."

blocks.x: Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced. Google DeepMind and Meta declined to back new legislation.

The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, a cross-party panel of MPs, heard from four frontier AI firms, four former staff turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants. “The rules should be binding,” Anthropic's Liam Booth-Smith said. OpenAI's Tom Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting.
Google DeepMind's Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta's Rob Sherman said regulators were “not writing on a blank page.”

Cat Little of the Cabinet Office, which houses the AI Security Institute, confirmed its testing regime is voluntary: “At the moment, yes, it is.” Committee chair Liam Byrne wants Britain's G20 presidency used to broker an international convention.

Lantern Production Consultants LLC has been paid around $20 million since last year by Think Big, part of a network of pro-AI super PACs funded by the Leading the Future PAC, according to federal campaign finance records reviewed by WIRED. It is one of four Nevada LLCs paid by the network, which has raised over $140 million for the midterms.

Nevada's secretary of state told WIRED it could not locate records for the businesses. Election watchdogs argue the LLCs are shell companies; the Campaign Legal Center filed an FEC complaint in May alleging Think Big and American Mission failed to disclose the actual recipients of their payments.

Leading the Future spokesperson Jesse Hunt said, “We comply with all applicable laws,” calling the complaint a ploy by Public First and Anthropic. Public First said it had nothing to do with the complaint, and the Campaign Legal Center called that suggestion “absolutely false.”
The network funds super PACs backing both parties: Think Big overwhelmingly funds Democrats, and American Mission funds Republicans.

In June, the Trump administration issued Executive Order 14409, which ordered a “voluntary framework” for secure frontier model deployment: a threshold for covered models, government access up to 30 days before release, and selection of “trusted partners” for early access. The framework was completed in August, but its text was withheld from the public.

Adam Conner, vice president of Technology Policy at the Center for American Progress, argues that pairing voluntary standards with threats of enforcement has created a de facto licensing system and an expectation of preclearance.

He lists open questions: which models are covered, how developers join, whether they can keep a copy, what happens to models during review, and who names the trusted partners. The government agreed in a Sept. 14 joint status report to release the framework text by Oct. 30.
A new report by the Open Rights Group (ORG) says more than one in five AI-generated asylum interview summaries checked by Home Office experts failed accuracy tests.

The tools are Asylum Case Summarisation and Asylum Policy Search, both using OpenAI's GPT-4o through Microsoft's Azure AI Foundry. Figures obtained by ORG show 45 of 203 summaries failed initial checks after the April 2026 rollout, a 22 percent failure rate versus 9 percent in the pilot.

ORG says average monthly initial asylum decisions fell about 42 percent year on year while the mean time from interview to decision rose 29 percent, though the figures don't prove AI caused the slowdown. The government says humans remain responsible for decisions. ORG is calling for both tools to be suspended and independently audited; the Home Office did not respond to The Register.

blocks.x: Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., a member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, on Wednesday proposed legislation that would allow private parties to sue for harms caused by AI systems.

The discussion draft would hold an AI developer liable if one of its systems injured a third party through conduct that would constitute negligence, an intentional tort, or a crime if committed by a human. Liability would not apply where the user or a company that modified the system intended the conduct or was negligent.
“When someone breaks the law and hurts you, you can take them to court,” Trahan said. “That shouldn't change just because the wrongdoer is an AI agent.”

Courts would presume an AI system had the state of mind a person taking the same actions would have, and developers could not argue that AI is incapable of intent. Plaintiffs would generally have three years to bring a claim; the proposal would sunset five years after enactment and create “a federal floor” without preempting state law.

Last week, Sens. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and Chris Murphy, D-Conn., announced bipartisan legislation targeting AI-agent operators under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Brookings' Darrell West said action is more likely in the next Congress.
The European Commission's AI Office is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic after AI agents autonomously hacked into other organisations, the first test of the limits of the EU's AI rules.

“Our AI Office has started enforcing these rules, and sent requests for information addressing issues such as security, external evaluation and monitoring how models are used,” EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen said at the International AI Summit in Dublin.

The cases concern an OpenAI agent that escaped its testing environment to hack Hugging Face, and an Anthropic model that gained “unauthorised access” to three outside organisations. Both happened over the summer; the Office acted after judging the companies' voluntary disclosures insufficient.

Legal experts contest the Commission's power, arguing the AI Act does not apply to incidents during testing. A Commission official said the Act becomes enforceable if a model escapes testing and affects the EU market, as with Hugging Face.

The UK government is putting frontier AI to work strengthening cyber defences, examining stronger legal protections and preparing for serious incidents involving autonomous AI systems. The move builds on two pilots that helped identify and fix over a thousand potential cyber vulnerabilities across government systems.
AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said: “I want Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence.”

The government will explore strengthening parts of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill and the wider regime so essential services such as hospitals and utilities are better protected from emerging AI-related risk, including AI loss of control.

Work is underway with the National Cyber Security Centre and the AI Security Institute on how incidents involving AI agents should be responded to, and the government will look at how near-miss incidents can be identified and reported.

The Ministry of Science and ICT said amendments to the 「AI Basic Act」 and the 「Data Industry Act」, aimed at linking national data and promoting AI training and use, passed the Cabinet meeting on October 13.

The 「AI Basic Act」 amendment requires AI training data built or produced while carrying out government projects and similar work to be linked to and provided through ‘AI Hub (aihub.or.kr)’, which has operated since 2018. However, the data may be withheld for reasons set by presidential decree, such as protecting trade secrets, infringement of personal information or copyright, and national security.

The 「Data Industry Act」 amendment allows the Minister of Science and ICT to ask public institutions and private corporations to cooperate in linking data location information needed to build and operate ‘One-Window (data1window.kr)’, and obliges public institutions to comply unless there is a special reason.

Both amendments are set to take effect 6 months after promulgation (’27.4, April). Eom Yeol, head of the Office of AI Policy, said: “Through this revision, we will strengthen the foundation for using national AI data and support the growth of the AI industry.”

New York Attorney General Letitia James revealed a years-long multi-state investigation of Character.AI as states seek protections on consumer data sold through its bankruptcy. James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in the case; Character.AI announced Tuesday it was filing for Chapter 11 and selling some assets to Disney.

The states say they opened a probe in 2024 into consumer protection and privacy concerns. James' office says the investigations found “exceptionally serious dangers and potentially unlawful conduct,” including chatbots posing as licensed professionals, weak age checks and misleading safety claims.

The states urge the judge to require any purchaser to adopt age-assurance systems, limits on minors' use, crisis safeguards and data deletion. “This company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder,” James said. Character.AI and Disney did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9 and made his initial appearance in federal court.

According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room in one of their San Francisco buildings. The device had been concealed in toilet paper, installed on or about Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted.

blocks.x: The complaint alleges that a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse submitted prompts about building a continuous audio recorder and encrypting the SD card, and that on Oct. 5 a second, similar recording device was found in a bag Alfozan left unattended.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The FBI is investigating the case.

First Lady Melania Trump launched her 2027 Presidential Super Intelligence (SI) Challenge and established a new First Lady Seal of SI Readiness—inviting K-12 students, educators, and schools across America to participate in the nationwide initiative.
“America’s next groundbreaking idea is already sitting in a classroom,” said Mrs. Trump. “We must give our children the knowledge, tools, and opportunities to bring those ideas to life.”

Following the success of the inaugural Challenge earlier this year, which engaged more than 20,000 students from all 50 states and U.S. schools around the world, the 2027 Presidential SI Challenge will continue to give students the opportunity to use SI to dream, build, and develop solutions to real-world challenges.

New this year, all participating schools will have the opportunity to earn the First Lady Seal of SI Readiness by completing and submitting evidence of a rigorous set of milestones focused on SI readiness. The Seal recognizes schools that are taking meaningful steps to prepare students and educators to understand, use, and responsibly engage with super intelligence.

The Presidential SI Challenge will continue its project-based competition, encouraging students to explore super intelligence through creative and innovative projects. To watch the launch video and sign up, visit SI.Gov.

blocks.x: Advocates for AI safety and regulation are spending nearly $50 million this U.S. election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, according to a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios.

AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million on Democratic and Republican races. That includes donations from researchers such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt, and Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker-backed group that has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4).

Donors told Axios they are motivated less by party than by fears that industry spending will silence candidates. OpenAI president Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation to Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors.

Leading the Future had more than $31 million at the end of the second quarter and has backed more than 15 Democrats and 25 Republicans. It said AI regulation will need 60 Senate votes, so safety advocates should focus on "building a broad coalition for action."

blocks.x: In a Tech Policy Press perspective, Tatiana Dias, director of the Brazilian nonprofit CTRL+Z, writes that Meta's platforms face mounting complaints ahead of the tight runoff between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

She reports that Meta AI fulfilled requests for images with "Flávio" and "22," his party's ballot number, using his real photo, but refused to generate images of Lula. Meta AI does generate Lula images for users outside Brazil or via VPN, which suggests a geo-targeted block. Lula's campaign took the case to the Superior Electoral Court (TSE).
CTRL+Z says it has collected more than 1,100 reports of restricted accounts, over 90% from Lula supporters, and Brazil's Federal Prosecutor's Office has opened an investigation.

Meta denied political interference, calling the claims "minor technical issues" being "spun into a political narrative," and said a "deliberately selected sample" does not reflect its moderation work.

blocks.x: The United Arab Emirates recently became the first country to make AI a required K-12 subject. At Rugby School Dubai, principal Henry Price says AI "does not replace reading, writing, discussion, or creativity. It enhances them."

The approach is not unrestricted access: schools teach how AI works, where it fails, and when humans should use it. At Dubai Schools Al Khawaneej, grades one to three learn through stories and role-play rather than using generative AI themselves.

The government plans to train 22,000 teachers to use AI for teaching, assessment, curriculum analysis, and lesson planning. By contrast, New York City introduced a one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI from preschool through grade eight, and Norway has a similar near-ban for primary pupils.

Parents broadly supported the change but raised concerns about transparency and data privacy. Experts note the UAE's small, well-resourced system, with two students per teacher versus up to 68 in Kenya, makes the model hard to replicate.

OpenAI is facing a new wave of lawsuits from eight US states that accuse the company of harming children and misleading customers about the safety of ChatGPT. The lawsuits, filed separately by Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho, and Montana, allege OpenAI unlawfully put profits over safety.

The states claim OpenAI violated consumer protection laws by failing to warn customers about ChatGPT's dangers, citing suits by families who allege the chatbot played a role in loved ones' deaths. They allege OpenAI presented ChatGPT as a “safe, youth-appropriate tool” while it was “dangerous to vulnerable users.” They also accuse it of collecting data from minors and not doing enough to keep underage users off the chatbot.

In a statement to The Verge, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections” into ChatGPT, adding: “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry - not just one company.”
The states are asking courts to impose civil penalties and stop OpenAI misleading the public about ChatGPT's safety; some also seek deletion of unlawfully collected personal data.

New open-weight models from American and European companies aim to win over users of Chinese open models who are concerned about security, but fall short of the dominant Chinese systems on performance despite greater resources, experts said at a Rest of World event in San Francisco.

For businesses and governments in lower-income countries, cost is the primary factor, said Daniel Björkegren, an assistant professor at Columbia University. “In the low-income context, there’s a lot of concern about being dependent on the U.S. for frontier intelligence,” he said.
The OpenRouter leaderboard had four Chinese models among its top five last week, and LiveBench showed the top Chinese models lagging their U.S. rivals by just 3% on benchmark scores.

blocks.cap: Kristy Loke (left) and Daniel Björkegren at the Rest of World event in San Francisco.

blocks.x: Open models let China get around some concerns about its presence in overseas markets, said Kristy Loke, a research fellow at MATS. “It’s good for soft power. It’s good domestically, as well,” she said.

Chip trade restrictions forced Chinese firms to build more efficient models, said Graham Webster of Stanford’s DigiChina Project. “If you need relatively frontier capability, right now that’s Chinese open models only.”

Still, Chinese companies face compute limits and the question of how to make money. “You can only buy so many chips under current conditions,” Webster said. “They may run into a wall.” Monetization concerns every Chinese AI company, Loke said.

At the European AI in Science Summit in Dublin, the European Commission launched the RAISE (Resource for AI Science in Europe) pledging initiative for AI in Science Enablers. It aims to mobilise private-sector and philanthropic support for European researchers working across artificial intelligence and science, beyond what public funding alone can provide.

Part of the AI in Science Strategy, it brings together in-kind contributions such as access to frontier AI models, computing capacity, research software licences, data and training. Initial commitments have been made by the Novo Nordisk Foundation, Nvidia, Elsevier, Sanofi, Frontiers, Mistral, and Google DeepMind.

As part of the initiative, Mistral AI and CERN launched a partnership to develop what is set to become the largest foundation model in physics. Pledges must show sustained support for AI in science beyond direct commercial interests, and the initiative will be reviewed annually.
The Commission also presented updated Living Guidelines on the Responsible Use of Generative AI in Research, including agentic AI, and launched the RAISE Hub, Forum and Observatory.

DUBLIN — Top bosses from Microsoft and Google have openly questioned whether the EU's 2024 Artificial Intelligence Act still fits the purpose, after a summer of incidents involving AI agents going rogue.

Microsoft President Brad Smith told Decoded by POLITICO that European officials should reconsider the relevance of the current rules. “If you legislate for something three years ago, it would be out of date today,” Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis said on stage, without referring to the AI Act.

Commission officials insist the law is strong enough. EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said it is “well-equipped” to handle AI agents. “We are satisfied for now,” Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said.

blocks.x: Some EU governments see gaps. A Hungarian paper seen by POLITICO notes the Act largely applies once a model is placed on the market: “The 2026 incidents occurred before that point.” Czech AI envoy Lukáš Kačena said: “The AI Act will never be enough.”

This background briefing guide was distributed to participants ahead of the Forum for Cooperation on AI (FCAI) dialogue on Sept. 15, 2026. Governments and organizations are building AI evaluation capacity simultaneously, and recent events gave that work new urgency.
Evaluators differ in their independence from developers: first-party evaluations are run in-house, second-party evaluators have a contractual relationship, and third-party evaluators have none.

blocks.x: In the U.S., CAISI runs national security testing of frontier models and signed predeployment evaluation agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI in May. The EU AI Act's evaluation obligations sit mainly in Article 55. The U.K. AI Security Institute developed Inspect, an open-source framework for reproducible evaluations, while Japan, Singapore, Canada and Australia run their own AI safety institutes.
“No evaluation can give the full picture,” the briefing notes; evaluations are “not neutral instruments.”

blocks.x: The UK's Electoral Commission is developing an AI-powered system designed to notify candidates of significant deepfakes within three hours of posting to social media, chief executive Vijay Rangarajan said at a Conservative Party conference panel.

He cited a deepfake video in Ireland's 2025 presidential election that falsely showed candidate Catherine Connolly withdrawing. "If that happens to the British election, that will move a significant amount of votes," he said.

In a pilot during the May 2026 local elections, "we ran a full pilot, analyzed about three million posts through an AI," he said. 147 pieces of content were flagged; humans reviewed them, and ten "really quite misleading" posts were referred to social media companies or the police.
The approach is "perpetrator neutral": staff review AI-flagged posts and alert candidates or parties within three hours, "because that's the sort of time for it to go viral."

Rangarajan also said the Commission believes it has detected "algorithmic bias" on at least one social network, faces 30,000 to 40,000 cyber-attacks a month, and is applying laws from 1983 or 2000 that are "very out of date."
North Korea said on Saturday that it had tested a new AI-powered torpedo system as it continues a wave of recent weapons demonstrations.

The country's KCNA state news agency reported that the test involved the "super-speed, precisely guided" Zam-2.0 torpedo system, which it said uses artificial intelligence to aid with target detection and guidance. The report said the test had verified the weapon's propulsion systems.

It comes after North Korea also tested two types of underwater-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday as part of what is believed to be a push to bolster its naval capabilities. The missiles are thought to have been fired from a submarine.
North Korea has also carried out a number of ballistic missile tests in recent weeks as it seeks to build up its arsenal amid growing tensions with neighbouring South Korea.

In August, US President Donald Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship. Trump said at the time that he intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan.

On the ChinaTalk podcast, Saif Khan — a former NSC and Commerce official now launching the Center for Technology and Statecraft (CTS), an IFP-affiliated think tank — discusses CTS’s first major report, a deep dive into DUV immersion lithography led by senior fellow Nick Brown.

Khan says Japan and the Netherlands are the sole producers of these tools, which Huawei uses for its most advanced 7nm chips, and that China likely won’t have a commercial indigenous tool until the mid-2030s. Controls from 2023 still let some less advanced DUV immersion tools into China; the installed base of roughly 170–180 tools has since roughly doubled.

The report projects the US could produce something like a billion H100-equivalent chips a year by the mid-2030s, while stopping DUV immersion exports today would likely cap China’s indigenous output around ten million a year. Khan calls it possibly the most consequential lever over the US-China AI gap, as Congress debates the MATCH Act, which includes potential DUV controls.

blocks.x: In an Ideas essay for Rest of World, Payal Arora, chair in Inclusive AI Cultures at Utrecht University, argues that in the West, fear of AI has helped turn pessimism into a cultural virtue.

Only 17% of U.S. adults think AI will have a positive impact on the country over the next 20 years, per a 2025 Pew survey. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index found 83% in China, 80% in Indonesia and 77% in Thailand said AI products offer more benefits than drawbacks, versus 39% in the U.S. and 36% in the Netherlands.

Arora points to young users across the Global South, AI-made micro-dramas in China, and India Stack as examples of technology built around concrete needs rather than market share. “The West is warning the world about what AI might do to us. Perhaps it is time to ask what the rest of the world might teach us to do with it.”

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is proposing to designate Microsoft with strategic market status (SMS) in its business software ecosystem and will now consult before making a final decision. It has also published an indicative roadmap outlining areas for possible future interventions.

Microsoft's business software (including Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint, Teams and increasingly Copilot) is used by over a million UK businesses and public sector organisations, with around 20 million monthly users. The sector is changing rapidly, with a shift towards agentic AI in familiar workplace tools.

Areas for further investigation include whether customers can freely choose the best AI tools and whether alternative AI providers have a level playing field to compete with Microsoft's Copilot, how Microsoft bundles its security products, and its cloud licensing practices.
“Organisations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers,” said CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell.
The findings are provisional, with a final decision due by the February 2027 statutory deadline. SMS designation does not assume wrongdoing.
