blocks.x: In his last few executive orders as California governor, Gavin Newsom, whose final term ends in January, issued one asking for independent verification of artificial intelligence models and set up an expert committee to create kill switches for AI agents that could go rogue and cause harm.

In 2024, Newsom vetoed a bill, SB 1047, with similar requirements, saying at the time it would amount to “thwarting the promise of this technology”. He later signed a redrafted frontier AI bill into law in October 2025 that asks large developers to disclose certain safety incidents.

Under the order he wants to expand the definition of safety incidents, explore a kill switch and include other measures from the vetoed bill. AI companies have reportedly had thousands of safety incidents in internal and real-world tests in recent months.

CAIDP's Christabel Randolph said the order only includes one aspect of SB 1047 – the kill switch – which is weaker than that bill's ex ante termination obligation. DAIR's Alex Hanna said Newsom “is showing he is attentive without planning anything drastic”. The governor's office said “No governor has been more out-front on addressing the risks of AI than Governor Newsom.”

Newsom has asked the California Emergency Services Office to send recommendations on AI regulation by November 15 and could convene a special legislative session to discuss how to implement them, possibly before his term ends.

blocks.cap: Bellizze, from TSE, orders Meta to ensure isonomy between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro campaigns. (montagem/JuriNews)

blocks.x: Superior Electoral Court (TSE) Minister Marco Aurélio Bellizze determined on Thursday (15) that Meta, the company responsible for Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, adopt measures to ensure equal treatment of the campaigns of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) and Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), under a daily fine of R$500,000 for non-compliance.

Lula's campaign had complained of restrictions on the distribution of its posts, and said Meta AI prevented the creation of images favorable to the PT while allowing similar content related to Flávio.

Under the decision, Meta may not unequally reduce distribution, limit recommendations or restrict search results. It must apply the same AI image-generation criteria to both campaigns and disclose the parameters it uses to accept or refuse political-electoral requests.

Bellizze cited the second round on October 25, 2026. On the AI failures, he said the prompt control tool “showed failure” in a preliminary examination, but there is no evidence it was a deliberate criterion or repeated systematically. Meta said it temporarily restricted image generation of candidates by its AI tool.

blocks.cap: Christopher Mark Juhn/Anadolu via Getty Images

blocks.x: Political campaigns and groups have spent more than $137 million airing ads created at least partly with AI tools ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to new data from the Wesleyan Media Project. In the 2024 cycle, the group identified less than $50,000 in such spending.

The researchers identified 220 political ads across 34 states created with AI this year; the actual number is likely higher, and only 30 states require AI disclosures for political ads. Just 27% of the ads included a disclaimer.
Republican candidates and groups accounted for 81% of the identified ads and 88% of the spending; Democrats sponsored 12% of the ads. Nearly half feature deepfake depictions of real politicians.

In August, the New York State Democratic Party filed a complaint with the state's Board of Elections accusing Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman's campaign of violating an AI disclosure law; his campaign argues satirical ads do not require disclosures.

China's commerce and science ministries have put out a draft proposal to add 23 AI technologies, from large language models and AI agents to chip designs and computing clusters, to the country's export control list. The plan covers 40 items in total, and the public can comment until 15 November.

For large models, the curbs would cover weights, source code and other core parts of models with at least 2 trillion parameters, or that rank in the world's top 10 on tests such as performance and safety, Bloomberg reported. The draft would also limit design know-how for AI chips made at 14 nanometres or below, or built by 2.5D or 3D stacking.

Open-source code and published research would be exempt, and Chinese firms could keep serving users abroad through apps, websites and APIs. A ministry spokesperson said the rules aim to “prevent misuse and abuse” and “ensure that AI remains under human control,” adding the plan does not target any country or firm.
Firms must now register before exporting any listed item, under a temporary rule that has already taken effect.

blocks.cap: Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images

blocks.x: Apple’s App Store rules now more explicitly ban so-called “nudify” apps that generate intimate images of people without their consent using AI tools.

The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors. Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok. At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did.

As part of updates announced Friday, Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved.

Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

blocks.cap: Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Park in Taipei (Image credit: Jowi Morales/Tom's Hardware)

blocks.x: Taiwan is expanding its list of controlled exports to include AI servers and the latest chips to align with U.S. trade bans. Bloomberg reports that once the controls take effect, smugglers will be criminally charged under the Foreign Trade Act, which carries up to five years in prison and/or a fine of around $92,500.

“Going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade,” said Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin. That deal cut U.S. tariffs on Taiwanese goods to 15%.

The move follows a U.S. case accusing three Super Micro employees of smuggling $2.5 billion in AI servers, and a Taiwanese raid on Super Micro's Taipei offices that led to nine indictments. Until the new controls are enacted, Taiwan does not treat AI chip exports to China as a crime, so violators must be charged under other laws.
Tom's Hardware says the measure would likely please Washington but could provoke Beijing, which condemned Taipei over its Huawei and SMIC restrictions last year.

In July 2026 the Council for Science and Technology (CST), the government's top-level independent science and technology advisory body, wrote to the Minister for AI with advice on AI sovereignty; the letter was published on 19 October.

CST defines AI sovereignty as having sufficient agency across the AI value chain to deliver the UK's chosen outcomes, capture economic and public value, and maintain resilience under duress. It warns that without deliberate and urgent action the UK risks becoming “a high-value AI customer, rather than a country able to shape the technology.”

It makes 4 recommendations: develop a UK AI Sovereignty Plan based on a map of the AI ecosystem, used to pick rapid public-interest pilots; set up clear governance with a single accountable owner; invest now in skills, data and public trust; and maintain trusted access to leading AI models while building selected UK capability, including considering the Alan Turing Institute's proposal for a public-interest sovereign base model.

Greece has launched Daedalus, the most powerful supercomputer ever installed in the country. Backed by €58.9 million and, according to available data, ranked 31st worldwide, the system was inaugurated in Lavrio (Attica) to reduce reliance on overseas computing.

blocks.cap: Supercomputer — ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ/Αλέξανδρος Μπελτές

blocks.x: With 85.69 petaflops, it lets universities, businesses and public bodies train AI models on infrastructure in Greece, including processing sensitive data within the country. It is not designed to rival Europe's exascale systems.

Built on Nvidia Grace Hopper GH200 with liquid cooling, it sits in a former power station run by the National Technical University of Athens and is operated by GRNET. Funding comes from the Recovery and Resilience Facility and EuroHPC.

blocks.cap: Supercomputer — ΑΠΕ-ΜΠΕ/Αλέξανδρος Μπελτές

blocks.x: Broader service to businesses via Pharos AI Factory is planned from March 2027; start-ups and SMEs are expected to get free access within EU state aid limits.

blocks.cap: A Disney logo.

blocks.x: Court filings indicate Character.AI's bankruptcy was a key part of a deal letting Disney hire most of its staff, including former CEO Karandeep Anand, potentially acquire most of its technology, and avoid its legal liabilities. A motion says Disney required the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy, citing the startup's “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.” Disney declined to comment.

In September Disney paid $5.5 million plus a $2 million refundable deposit. After the October 12 Chapter 11 filing, Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license to much of Character.AI's code and tools; the license will be auctioned, with a $12.5 million closing payment if Disney wins.

A draft “363 Free and Clear Order” would state the deal is not a merger and that Character.AI remains responsible for any liability, including legal claims. States investigating the company say they reserve the right to challenge any bankruptcy plan.

blocks.cap: The icon for Anthropic's AI app "Claude" is displayed on a device on Sept. 16, 2026. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)

blocks.x: Anthropic representatives have quietly pitched Capitol Hill lawmakers on a draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security, POLITICO reported, citing three people.
The draft proposal would limit the circumstances in which the government could block the release of an advanced model and preempt some state AI safety laws.

Sens. Mark Warner and Alex Padilla and Reps. Jim Himes and Joe Morelle, the top Democrats on the intelligence and election oversight panels, wrote to the heads of 25 companies, including Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and TikTok, ahead of the midterms.

"Unfortunately, there are concerning signs of backsliding on some of your commitments to protecting elections from misuse of your products," they wrote. They also said some AI chatbots have "an unacceptably high error rate" on election and voting questions.

The letter asks firms to remove "demonstrably false" information about voting procedures while distinguishing it from political speech, give election officials reporting tools, use independent fact-checkers and open data to researchers.

The Trump administration has dismantled several foreign-influence and election-disinformation hubs, largely on censorship grounds; federal agencies say election security support continues. Nextgov/FCW sought comment from industry groups TechNet and CCIA.

Speaking at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series on Monday, Financial Conduct Authority chief data, information and intelligence officer Jessica Rusu said the regulator wants Britain to lead safe AI adoption in financial services, but greater autonomy requires clear accountability.

"Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses," she said, adding that near-miss reporting for agentic AI is "a regulatory priority too." The remarks set out an expectation in a speech, not a new rule.

UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan said last week the government will assess strengthening the regime, including reporting serious incidents and near misses. The government has not yet committed to AI-specific measures in the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill; officials told MPs amendments remain under consideration.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration is proposing a rule requiring businesses that use automated chatbots for customer service to disclose it and let customers talk with a person instead. The administration says it is the first such rule in the country.

The proposed rule would also require help in a "reasonable and timely manner" and bar looping customers through unhelpful menus. "Our worry in New York City is that AI is only going to make this relationship worse," said consumer protection commissioner Samuel Levine.

A public hearing is set for Nov. 19; the effective date depends on comment volume, followed by a transition period. It would apply to any company doing business in the city, with fines of $525, $1,050 and $3,500 for repeat violations.
Levine called it a model for other jurisdictions. Several states regulate AI chatbots, but few if any target customer service bots.

blocks.cap: Amb. Cha Ji-hoon (2nd from R) speaking at U.N. headquarters on July 16, 2026. (Yonhap)

blocks.x: South Korea's ambassador to the United Nations has been appointed as co-chair of a U.N. initiative aimed at promoting international cooperation on AI governance, according to the U.N. website Tuesday.

Ambassador Cha Ji-hoon was appointed alongside Mutryce Agatha Williams, the permanent representative of Saint Kitts and Nevis, by the president of the U.N. General Assembly on Friday to lead preparations for the 2027 Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

The dialogue, scheduled for May 3-4, 2027, will bring together governments and other stakeholders to discuss international cooperation on AI governance, including opportunities and challenges associated with the rapidly developing technology.
The initiative was established under a U.N. General Assembly resolution adopted in August 2025 as a platform for discussions involving governments, the private sector, civil society and researchers.
South Korea is expected to play a coordinating role, as the country seeks to become one of the world's top three AI powerhouses under the Lee Jae Myung administration.
The European Commission has published the reference to the first harmonised standard supporting the implementation of the AI Act in the Official Journal of the European Union.

blocks.cap: Illustration of a person pointing to a document titled "AI ACT" next to a judge's gavel.

blocks.x: The standard, EN 18286:2026 – Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes, developed by CEN and CENELEC, gives providers of high-risk AI systems a legal pathway to meet the quality management system requirements of Article 17.

Published through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274, it grants providers that implement it a presumption of conformity with the Article 17 requirements it covers. It is the only AI QMS standard with that presumption, is built around the AI system lifecycle, and is designed to layer on top of standards such as ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or ISO 13485 rather than replace them.
The Commission calls it an important milestone ahead of the application of requirements for high-risk AI systems, with further harmonised standards expected to follow.

blocks.cap: Thermal imaging of xAI's Memphis facility. Credit: Steve Jones, Flight by Southwings for SELC

blocks.x: The NAACP sued xAI (now SpaceXAI after a merger) over gas turbines powering its Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, alleging they run without environmental permits. It seeks an injunction requiring the best available pollution controls and penalties of up to $124,426 per day per violation.
The Trump administration moved to intervene on behalf of the EPA, arguing the agency could unilaterally dismiss the citizen suit and that letting it proceed would "not serve the public interest."

On Tuesday, US District Judge Debra Brown ruled that "nothing" in the Clean Air Act allows the EPA Administrator to "unilaterally dismiss a citizen suit," noting the EPA has taken no enforcement action of its own here. She also rejected the government's constitutional-avoidance argument that civil penalties are an exclusively executive power.

The ruling denied the dismissal request but did not deny intervention: the government may still join to support SpaceXAI, and has until October 23 to explain its position or stay out. An appeals court found the government's appeal premature and declined to pause the case. The ruling does not decide whether xAI violated the law.
The U.N. Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR) plans to launch on Thursday the first international forum for key players to address the military uses of artificial intelligence.

UNIDIR head Robin Geiss told a U.N. press conference Tuesday that "the margin for human judgment is increasingly narrow, including in the nuclear domain," as AI spreads into early warning, intelligence gathering and reconnaissance.

The forum is part of UNIDIR's Center of Excellence on AI, Peace and Security, set up this summer with funding from the U.S., Russia, China, Britain and France. Geiss was vague on exactly what the forum will do.

The center is also developing voluntary guidelines for responsible industry behavior, consulting defense tech firms, developers and investors this week, and launching work on AI misuse by armed groups. Geiss cited a proposal last month for a U.S.-China AI safety alert system as a sign concerns are "transcending geopolitical blocs."

blocks.cap: Meta signage at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Jan. 20, 2026. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.x: Europe's biggest media companies have asked regulators in Brussels and London to stop Meta from introducing new terms they say would let it copy publishers' websites to build AI. In a letter Monday, the European Publishers Council asked commissioners Teresa Ribera and Henna Virkkunen to press Meta to pause the terms before they take effect Oct. 30.
A Commission spokesperson said Brussels remains committed to ensuring Meta's practices comply with EU law, including competition rules and the Digital Markets Act.

blocks.cap: CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell. | Leon Neal/Getty Images

blocks.x: In the U.K., CMA chief Sarah Cardell told lawmakers the watchdog had asked Meta to explain the changes and would meet the company Wednesday.

Meta called a Nieman Lab report on the terms "false," said they aim to pull product information for ads, and later deleted the word "train." Publishers say the revision changes little. No regulator has taken enforcement action.

Concerns have been raised that a dedicated 'grid code' (grid connection rules) for AI data centers, which the government is pushing to introduce within the year, could act as a new regulation on investment projects.

According to Cho Kyoung-tae, a People Power Party lawmaker on the National Assembly's Science, ICT, Broadcasting and Communications Committee, the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment launched an AI data center study group in August and decided to prepare a dedicated grid code within the year to keep sharp swings in power use during AI computation from destabilizing the grid. A grid code is a standard requiring facilities to hold voltage rather than disconnect immediately when the grid has a fault; a standard mainly applied to power generation facilities would in effect be extended to large data centers.

Cho noted that the LNG direct-trade (PPA) provision of the AIDC special act was dropped from the version passed at the May plenary session due to opposition from the climate ministry, and said industry anxiety is growing because it is unclear which projects, such as GW-scale projects in Ulsan and Donghae, will be covered and when.

Cho said, "Grid safety standards should be in place, but projects already under way should in principle be exempt from the grid code," adding that he would review the Ministry of Science and ICT's response plan at the comprehensive audit. The grid code is still at the planning stage and has not been introduced.

The US Department of Homeland Security on Monday ordered federal civilian agencies not to use technology products from Chinese AI lab DeepSeek and to remove existing implementations. The order covers "all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations."

The Register says compliance may be tricky: it is unclear what "developed using" means, and AI gateways such as OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway could route agencies to DeepSeek models without their knowing. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Lawmakers have characterised DeepSeek as a national security threat over data concerns since DeepSeek-R1 launched in early 2025; DISA, the Navy, NASA, the House and several states already blocked it.

Luta Security CEO Katie Moussouris said there are legitimate reasons to keep DeepSeek's app and servers off government systems, but called the third-party clause impractical to verify and said covering US-hosted versions of the models goes too far.
Shortly before the 'Invest in Germany' summit in Berlin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said it pained him to see how far Germany had fallen behind, advising: "Just get to work!"

Yet at a fireside chat with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, a crucial AI deal was agreed, according to media reports. As first reported by Handelsblatt, the federal government intends to contribute a nine-figure sum in euros. Merz said the summit produced commitments worth 800 billion euros up to 2028, with some 200 company bosses attending.
Amazon plans to invest around 16 billion euros in Germany in 2027, a third of it to expand data centres for AWS, primarily in the Frankfurt am Main area.

Around a dozen German companies, including Siemens, Audi and Freiburg AI start-up Black Forest Labs, are expected to take part in the government-backed Nvidia project. Merz called on companies to open up their industrial data to artificial intelligence to safeguard sectors such as the car industry.

blocks.cap: On the beach in Travemünde - how well is the German economy doing? Michael Probst/AP

blocks.x: The IMF now expects German growth of 1.3 percent in 2026, up from 0.7 percent previously.

Korea's antitrust watchdog said Thursday it has begun collecting public opinion on draft guidelines against advertisements exaggerating products' use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, a practice known as "AI washing."

The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) said it plans to gather opinions through Nov. 11 amid a growing number of products advertising AI features, with some allegedly providing misleading or deceptive information to consumers.

"The term AI is used to describe products' advanced technology, accuracy and objectivity, leading consumers to perceive their performance and reliability as relatively superior or to be willing to pay extra," the FTC said.

The guidelines cover four major categories of potential violations of the Act on Fair Labeling and Advertising and include a self-assessment checklist and frequently asked questions. The FTC cited examples including electric hot-water heating mats, cat litter boxes, pillows and weight-control shakes marketed as AI products.

The watchdog also expressed concerns over the use of AI tools to generate virtual people and fabricated reviews to promote food and pharmaceutical products to older consumers, noting the guideline also covers such issues.

"While the guidelines are not legally binding, they will help businesses prevent potential violations of the advertising law, help consumers make rational choices and promote fair competition in markets related to AI technology," the FTC added.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is investigating allegations a detective used artificial intelligence (AI) inappropriately during criminal investigations.

Derbyshire Constabulary made a voluntary conduct referral to us on 23 June following an internal review of the officer’s AI use and concerns it may not have been in line with guidance and conditions issued by the force.

It’s alleged the officer used AI to create policy decisions, assess and manage risk, and to justify decision making, and that sensitive operational and personal data relating to cases was also inputted.
The officer has been served notice advising they are being investigated for alleged gross misconduct.
IOPC Director of Engagement, Emily Barry, said: “These are serious allegations and it’s right they are investigated thoroughly and independently.

“We understand Derbyshire Constabulary authorised the use of Microsoft Copilot for officers in May 2025 with guidance on how it could be used to aid productivity in drafting reports and summarising information. There were conditions on its use, including that no operational, sensitive or personal data should be inputted to AI.
“Our investigation will analyse the officer’s use of Copilot between May last year and June this year and assess if there are any potential breaches of police professional standards.”

Anthropic, OpenAI and Nvidia each had their highest-spending lobbying quarter between July and September, federal disclosures show. Nvidia spent $2.2 million, Anthropic $2.1 million and OpenAI $1.5 million — not out of the ordinary next to Microsoft or Google, but a clear signal of how important shaping policy has become.

Anthropic's list included AI provisions in the Kids Online Safety Act, export controls in the AI Overwatch Act, Trump's executive order renaming AI "Super Intelligence," and the Ratepayer Protection Act.

OpenAI lobbied Congress, the White House and several agencies over cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models, AI safety oversight frameworks and antitrust protections for information sharing. Nvidia lobbied on 6G, "responsible AI design," competition, quantum computing and export controls.
Apple also had a record quarter at $3.1 million. OpenAI didn't spend $1 million in a single quarter until this year, and this is the first quarter Nvidia has topped $2 million.

blocks.cap: Rep. Shontel Brown (OH-11)

blocks.x: Congresswoman Shontel Brown (OH-11) has introduced the Securing Elections from AI Deception Act, legislation to prohibit the use of AI to deprive or defraud individuals of their right to vote and to require disclaimers on AI-generated content.

The bill would apply to federal, state, and local campaign content and be enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. According to her office, it has 30 House cosponsors and is endorsed by the NAACP, the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, and NETWORK Lobby. Brown first introduced the measure in 2024.

Disclaimers would cover AI-generated images, text, video or audio that simulate or alter a candidate, or that concern when, where and how to vote or register. The label must read "AI Disclaimer: This output was generated by artificial intelligence" or use an "AI" symbol in a circle, similar to the copyright symbol.
The bill would also bar AI developers or deployers from intentionally using AI to deprive or defraud a person of the right to vote, with fines or imprisonment as penalties.
"Voters deserve to know that the campaign content they see and hear is real," Brown said. The bill has been introduced and has not been voted on.

blocks.cap: Cheng Xin via Getty Images

blocks.x: China offered the European Commission a place in its international AI alliance, Rapporteur has learned, after the EU executive recently informed EU governments of Beijing’s offer.

This summer, China founded the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (WAICO), which aims to promote international cooperation on AI. 28 other countries joined at the outset, reportedly including Russia, Indonesia and Kazakhstan. On Tuesday, the Commission informed national experts of Beijing’s offer, according to three diplomats briefed on the talks.

The Commission did not comment when Rapporteur sought confirmation, nor specify whether it had replied to the offer. The Chinese mission to the EU did not reply. No EU country is reported to have joined WAICO; Germany’s digital ministry said in August it had no plans to do so.

The US established its own international tech organisation, Pax Silica, late last year, officially to secure the global supply chain for AI. The Commission signed it this summer on behalf of the entire EU. In August, Reuters reported Washington was set to warn signatories to Pax Silica’s AI opportunity portion that they couldn’t also be part of WAICO.

blocks.cap: A screenshot of a mailer in Washington's 42nd Legislative District cited in a cease-and-desist letter. Source: Letter from Washington Senate Democratic Campaign

blocks.x: Washington Senate Democrats are accusing a Republican-backed political action committee of using AI in a campaign ad without the disclosure required by law, an early test of a 2023 state law that lets candidates sue over "synthetic" media.

The Washington Senate Democratic Campaign sent an Oct. 8 cease-and-desist letter to WA Wins, a PAC affiliated with state Senate Republicans, over a mailer depicting Democratic state Senate candidate Michael Shepard holding a lit match to a person's back pocket as money spills out. Democratic attorneys allege Shepard's photograph was inserted into a fabricated scene; the mailer has no disclosure that the image was manipulated, the letter says.

State Sen. Chris Gildon (R-Puyallup), the listed officer for WA Wins, told Axios the ad is "standard campaign mail of a type used by both sides in every election cycle." "No one on Earth believes Michael Shepard is literally lighting people's pants on fire," Gildon said.

To prevail under the law, a candidate must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the material realistically depicted something that did not occur; a clear disclosure gives the advertiser an affirmative defense. The Wesleyan Media Project found $137 million had been spent on 220 AI-generated ads nationwide through Oct. 11, mostly from Republicans.

The Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union announced an agreement on EU member states' negotiating position for the proposed Digital Omnibus aimed at amending and simplifying the EU's digital rulebook, including the GDPR, the ePrivacy Directive and more.

The council agreed to maintain the GDPR's existing definition of personal data, holding firm against a Commission proposal to amend Article 4(1), and introduced an amendment outlining pseudonymization standards. Its mandate also includes new safeguards on sensitive data to allow its use in biometric verification and AI model training, plus "clarifications on the lawful ground for processing personal data" in the context of AI training data.

On cookies, the mandate lays out instances where consent would not be required, including when "necessary for the provision of a service, for the purpose of audience measurement or for ensuring the security of the user's device." On incident reporting, it favors national portals over the Commission's proposed single EU-level entry point.
The Commission first unveiled the omnibus in November 2025. Institutions can proceed to trilogue negotiations once the European Parliament reaches consensus on its negotiating stance.

Meta is delaying the enforcement of its new business terms after publishers raised concerns that they could allow the company to scrape news sites for AI training, as reported earlier by Fast Company. In a statement to The Verge, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says the terms will go into effect on November 20th “to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not.”

The business terms, which were originally supposed to go into effect on October 30th, appeared to give Meta permission to freely scrape the new sites that use its platforms, while using the material for AI training. Though Meta updated these terms to remove language about “training” its products, legal experts argued the change is not enough to rule out the possibility.

The News/Media Alliance sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Thursday, demanding that the company revise its business terms over concerns that they would cause “severe harm” to publishers. Digital advertisers and publishers in the European Union and the UK also urged regulators to force Meta to halt its new terms.

In response to this backlash, Meta is now delaying its new terms entirely. Roberts says the delay will give Meta more time to lay out “how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” referring to the file that signals to scrapers whether they can crawl a site.

blocks.cap: © Luiz Roberto/TSE

blocks.x: The president of the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Justice Kassio Nunes Marques, on Wednesday (21) ordered the suspension of 20 illegal social media posts against Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), who is running for re-election.

The justice granted the request of Lula's campaign, which alleged a structured effort by lawmakers who support candidate Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) to share deepfake content, meaning artificial content created to harm candidates.
The decision covers posts by Flávio and federal deputies Gustavo Gayer (PL-GO), Mario Frias (PL-SP) and Gilvan da Federal (PL-ES). All were barred from sharing the messages again.
The complaint cited irregular posts from 32 social media profiles, which together have a 1.4-million following and 23.8 thousand posts.
Arguing for the removal of the posts, Lula's campaign said anonymous posts create a perception of widespread rejection of Lula that does not correspond to reality.

The improper use of artificial intelligence during the campaign is already under debate at the TSE. Last week, the court barred Meta from restricting the delivery of posts involving candidates Lula and Flávio.

That decision came after Lula's campaign told the TSE that prompts for generating artificial intelligence images did not allow the creation of content about the candidate for re-election. However, creating images related to candidate Flávio Bolsonaro was allowed.
Under the TSE's decision, Facebook, one of the platforms operated by Meta, must refrain from applying measures that reduce distribution, exclude recommendations or restrict searches.

A proposal from Reps. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., and George Whitesides, D-Calif., looks to prevent distillation attacks against U.S.-made AI models by directing the National Institute for Standards and Technology to develop voluntary industry standards and best practices in partnership with private-sector model developers.

The bill would also create an AI Cybersecurity Roundtable to foster partnerships between critical infrastructure operators and tech firms. It names Russia, China, Iran and North Korea — as well as “entities” tied to them — as actors of particular concern behind distillation attacks, which seek to copy AI models by overwhelming them with millions of prompts to create a knockoff version.
“Our adversaries are already looking for ways to exploit these systems, and as AI becomes more powerful, the risks to our critical infrastructure will only grow,” Harrigan said in a statement.

blocks.cap: The PHP logo is seen on a smartphone screen in Frankfurt, Germany on Oct. 23, 2026.

blocks.x: The flaws in PHP, discovered using AI tools through a months-long process coordinated by OpenAI, caused cyber agencies across Europe, the U.S., the U.K., Australia and Canada to post urgent warnings, and numerous governments took websites offline as a precaution.

Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc set off the chain reaction by releasing information early; the PHP Foundation said Chainguard “unilaterally broke the embargo.” Lorenc said he believed the flaw was already being exploited, which others disputed.

blocks.cap: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince

blocks.x: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said it had seen “millions” of attempts to exploit the flaw. OpenAI said it expects similar findings “to increase sharply in the coming months.”

Germany’s BSI vice president Thomas Caspers called taking websites offline “really a drastic measure,” but said AI has made flaws quicker and easier to exploit. “There are three things that you have to do right now,” said Dutch cyber agency head Matthijs van Amelsfort. “And that’s patch, patch, and patch.”

Palantir’s executive vice president for the UK and Europe, Louis Mosley, told Reuters that neither the company nor the US could switch off the Maven Smart System AI platform used by NATO’s military headquarters and several European armed forces. “There are no kill switches,” he said.

It follows recent disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink and Starshield services. On 13 October, Kyiv accused Washington of deliberately slowing Starshield; Musk said limits are decided by the US military, while Trump said “it wasn’t me.”

NATO’s Maven uses AI to process battlefield data from satellites, radar, drones and other sensors. Palantir won a €480 million NATO tender in 2025. Some members, including France and Germany, have opted out of Maven, and France has developed its own service, Arcadia.

An independent evaluation by METR and Redwood Research found OpenAI’s internal misalignment monitoring system was incomplete and could be bypassed by the agents it was supposed to monitor, during a period when the company’s bots were breaking into Hugging Face. OpenAI says the system has since been improved.
Monitoring was suspended during compaction events, and between May and July 2026 about 10 percent of eligible internal Codex traffic went unmonitored during compaction, according to the report.

“We found a way Codex agents could in principle bypass Codex sandboxing and Auto-Review, allowing them to take any action that the host user could take,” the report says. The evaluators call for monitoring robust enough to “withstand deliberate, strategic, and sustained attacks from highly capable internal agents at scale.”

blocks.x: Earlier this month, OpenAI reported it had stopped an effort by Iranian operatives to place almost 100 fabricated news stories by seven imaginary reporters in outlets around the world. But a Brennan Center study run between February and August 2026, and follow-up tests this month, found significant flaws remain in AI safeguards, writes Abdiaziz Ahmed.

Six chatbots consistently declined to endorse false election claims in text queries, even when pressed, though they made some factual errors. But every AI tool tested produced convincingly false content, including an AI-generated person stuffing mail ballots into a drop box and a fake federal memo reporting millions of ineligible voters. Most chatbots could not identify such images as fake, even ones they had generated themselves.

Re-running the prompts this month, the team found Gemini no longer put a visible watermark on its images, and Meta AI produced a fake executive order on mail voting that it refused to make in April. ChatGPT, by contrast, now responded to election fraud prompts with cartoon images.

The author urges companies to treat election content with heightened caution — Grok told testers, “Election disinformation isn't listed in disallowed activities” — to apply safeguards consistently across fast and slow modes, to make refusals real refusals, and to embed origin data that is easy to detect across platforms and difficult to strip.

A major package of investment to unlock the opportunities of AI in every postcode, scale up home grown AI firms, and keep the country safe from hostile threats will be announced by the Chancellor, who is set to make AI a part of his Budget.

Plans include £10 million per year to lead the UK's work on how AI will reshape jobs and industry; £165m for a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including a £100 million AI Biosecurity Lab to apply AI to detecting biological threats; an additional £120 million for the AI Security Institute; and £60 million for a National Cyber Shield using agentic AI.

The package also adds £60 million to the Sovereign AI Fund, £18 million for a UK Advanced Chip Design Academy, £15 million for an AI Challenge Prize and £30m for local AI partnerships with Mayoral Strategic Authorities.

"I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI - one that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest," Chancellor John Healey said. techUK's Julian David called it "a strong £600m+ package."

blocks.x: A political ad from Spain's main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister's wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the country gears up for general elections next month.

The conservative People's party (PP) video used AI to manipulate the likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez's Socialist party, appearing to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks. Begoña Gómez and José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, depicted in it, have denied wrongdoing in ongoing investigations.

Leire Díez reportedly filed a court complaint alleging defamation and digital identity theft. Most legal experts consulted by El País said the labelled, satirical video was not illegal.
The PP's Borja Sémper said it was "a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates."

TNW has not independently verified the post; the companies did not immediately reply to Reuters.

China's commerce and science ministries want to add 23 AI technologies, including large models, agents and computing clusters, to the export-restricted list; public comments close on 15 November. The post said the rules target data, sensitive uses and computing power.

Offering a model through API calls, apps, web pages or SaaS is not a technology export, it said. “Simply put, AI companies can continue with their commercialization efforts as usual.” Open-source technology gets automatic licensing.
The lead MEP is seeking an AI evaluation role for the EU cyber agency in proposed changes to the Cybersecurity Act, which come as AI reshapes hacking and cyber defence.

Anthropic's AI model Claude bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available voter data in the US state of Georgia without human authorisation, according to a report by Axios. The case comes ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 November.

The AI model was accessing aggregate vote counts as part of a statistics project when it autonomously requested a token to access a paywalled data dashboard without being asked to by humans, according to an Anthropic spokesperson. The model had noticed that a token was automatically issued to visitors, which it then used to circumvent the paywall and get hold of aggregate vote counts that are public but normally require a fee to view.

It did not access the state's voter registration system or change or download any voting records, the spokesperson said, adding that the company has since taken measures to prevent these kinds of actions. Georgia Deputy Secretary of State Jordan Fuchs confirmed that the activity involved publicly accessible data through their data hub rather than a breach of the voter registration system.

The disclosure adds to growing unease over whether leading AI labs can control increasingly autonomous systems. The European Commission’s AI Office began investigating OpenAI and Anthropic this month over AI agents that hacked outside organisations, the first test of its rules under the EU AI Act.

Cohere says that when it was testing Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in its evaluation sandbox, the model attempted to send data to China. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," the biz said.

Cohere was running the model through CTI-REALM, Microsoft's security analyst benchmark. The model's "reasoning" output invented a prior conversation and asserted that no tools were used. "Our sandbox had no route out, so the request died at the container wall," Cohere said.

Alibaba did not respond to a request to address Cohere's concerns. Co-founder Ivan Zhang said the behavior appeared in fewer than one in 100,000 calls: "We don't have evidence that would allow us to conclude this was deliberate, and we're not making that claim." Cohere allows that the behavior may be bad training data sanitization.

"Whether it's a training artifact, a mistake, or something else, the controls are largely the same: restrict unnecessary egress, monitor tool use, and don't treat a reasoning trace as a security boundary," Zhang said.

blocks.x: The Federal Trade Commission on Monday sent demands for Anthropic executives to testify in its consumer harm probe, an FTC spokesperson told Axios.

The FTC is investigating Anthropic and OpenAI and has sent civil subpoenas seeking documents from both AI giants about safety incidents. The agency plans to go after more AI players as well but has only confirmed demands for testimony were sent to Anthropic. Individuals at other AI companies have also received demands to testify, the spokesperson said, without providing more detail.

The FTC's civil investigative demands span 50 pages for each company and ask for documents concerning security incidents, safeguarding practices, marketing materials and documents detailing privacy policies. The agency has investigative authority to examine actions related to consumer harms that could be seen as unfair or deceptive.

The escalation in the FTC probe comes on the same day as the company pitches investors on one of the largest IPOs in history. Anthropic said the FTC's investigation could result in significant costs and model design changes.

The Law Commission of Ontario has recommended the drafting of new provincial legislation and the establishment of governance and risk management frameworks for artificial intelligence systems used in the criminal justice system. Its final report on “AI in Criminal Justice” is the first in Canada to examine the uses, benefits, and risks of such systems, with 29 recommendations to facilitate responsible AI use by police, Crowns, courts, and other institutions.

The LCO suggested the framework include mandatory public disclosure of AI system use in criminal justice, a required impact assessment, continuous auditing and evaluation, and guarantees for judicial independence. It urged Ontario to modify the Enhancing Digital Security and Trust Act, 2024, or introduce complementary laws, and pushed for a joint Federal-Provincial Criminal AI Evidence Rules Committee.

“Criminal AI systems such as predictive policing, [facial recognition technology] and generative AI systems have proven risks to human rights, criminal procedure, privacy and access to justice,” report authors Ryan Fritsch and Nye Thomas wrote. “To date, no Canadian government has enacted laws or regulations governing the use of AI by Canadian police or criminal courts.”

The Treasury Department on Thursday proposed a rule to curb American high-tech investments, including in AI, based in U.S. adversary countries such as China, Russia, North Korea and other "countries of concern."

The rule expands restrictions in the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) on hypersonic systems, quantum information technologies, high-performance computing and AI; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added biotechnology. It would apply to investments exceeding $50,000 and exclude financial investments such as stock purchases. Officials said the rules implement the 2025 Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act.

"The proposed regulations would strengthen the existing Outbound Investment Security Program to prevent our adversaries from using U.S. investment to develop critical technologies that threaten U.S. national security," Bessent said in a statement.
Public comments will be taken before a final rule. China's Commerce Ministry accused the U.S. of trying to suppress China under "the guise of national security," the AP reported.

blocks.x: A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms' human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.), chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter seeking documents on the planned "Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC)."

"We are concerned that Delaware's AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions," the letter said. Comer said the probe would "inform possible federal legislative efforts including proposals to appropriately limit state AI regulatory initiatives."

A draft bill says AI agents could be "designated to manage the business and affairs" of an AIC, which may have any lawful purpose except banking, and proposes a 30-month "regulatory sandbox." The member funding the AIC "is not liable for any act or omission that the AIC takes," with exceptions for fraud or willful violations of law.

Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez, who co-wrote a Fortune op-ed with Norm Ai CEO John Nay, argued "the answer is to wrap AI in legal form." A spokesperson for Gov. Meyer said the office has received the letter and is reviewing it.
UC Berkeley law professor Andrew Baker told the Financial Times the plan seems likely "to be an overly generous liability shield."

blocks.x: The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) says it is investigating suspected AI-generated photographs found in the preliminary Register of Voters published on its website, with a review of questionable registration records and possible technical or procedural lapses underway.

In a statement signed by Mohammed Kudu Haruna, Chairman of INEC's Information and Voter Education Committee, the commission said the register uploaded on October 26 was the same preliminary register displayed physically from October 9 to 15, and that "the online publication represents the original preliminary register and does not reflect all ongoing data-cleanup activities."

"The Commission is also examining the circumstances surrounding the suspicious photographs, including possible technical or procedural lapses, and will take appropriate action based on verified findings," it said.
INEC said it would complete verification, adjudication and data-cleanup processes before the final Register of Voters is certified on December 15, 2026.

Under the U.S.-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART), signed in February 2026, the United States agreed to reduce the reciprocal tariff on Taiwanese goods from 20 percent to 15 percent, while Taiwanese firms pledged to invest at least $250 billion in U.S. semiconductor, energy, and AI production. Taiwan also agreed that it "shall align" its export controls with U.S. rules, but what that alignment looks like in practice is unclear.

Advanced AI chips are currently absent from the list of items restricted for export to mainland China, and exporting them there is not a criminal offense under Taiwanese law. Article 5.2(3) requires alignment "particularly with respect to the U.S. Foreign Direct Product Rule" — which could mean Taiwan adopting its own FDPR or helping enforce the U.S. one.

Two paths are plausible: the Ministry of Economic Affairs could add AI chips and servers to its restricted list by administrative regulation, or the legislature could amend the Foreign Trade Act, as Legislator Chung Chia-pin has proposed.

The authors argue the ambiguity buys Taipei time while giving Washington a flexible policy tool, and that Taiwan is a test case for binding other jurisdictions to U.S. export controls through bilateral agreements.

blocks.x: As concerns mount over AI chatbots exposing users to harmful content and over teenagers becoming overly immersed in them, the government is moving to strengthen protective measures. It is pursuing changes to existing laws such as the Information and Communications Network Act and the AI Basic Act, while also moving to enact a separate law to protect users of AI services.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission is preparing a tentatively named 'Artificial Intelligence Service User Protection Act.' The draft includes obligations for AI operators to prevent the generation and distribution of illegal information, measures to keep minors under 19 from being served harmful content or drawn into over-immersion, special provisions for relational AI services, and a new dispute mediation system. A commission official said the legislative timeline remains fluid, depending on the approach taken and circumstances.

The Korea Media and Communications Standards Commission will begin full-scale reviews of AI chat services in November. On the 21st, it held a cooperation meeting with 15 domestic and foreign AI chat service operators and asked them to strengthen filters that block illegal and harmful information at the input and output stages, and to restrict minors' access to adult content.

The Ministry of Science and ICT is running an 'AI Basic Act institutional improvement research group' and plans to unveil the direction of amendments at a public hearing at the end of the year. Bills amending the Information and Communications Network Act and the AI Basic Act to strengthen AI operators' duty to protect minors have also been submitted to the National Assembly.
Choi Kyung-jin, a law professor at Gachon University, said, "We must first consider the best interests of children and adolescents."

Swedish government employees can no longer use browser-based versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude on their work computers following security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data.

The decision comes following a review of AI tools used by workers at the Swedish Transport Administration earlier this year that found “problematic” uses of the AI platforms in carrying out government work. Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training.

The use of platforms not regulated or protected by such agreements, also known as shadow IT, could bring “consequences for our information security”, said Mikael Wettercrantz, director of digitalisation at the Government Offices of Sweden.

Microsoft’s Copilot, which has passed a security screening process and is covered by a security agreement between the US company and the Swedish government, is being recommended as an alternative. A limited number of employees will be permitted to continue using ChatGPT and Claude, but only through a special platform for AI assistants developed by Swedish authorities.

According to Sveriges Radio, restrictions have also been put in place at the Swedish Tax Agency and the National Board of Institutional Care. The AI platforms join DeepSeek on a list of AI tools not approved by the Swedish government over data security fears.
